spots.name: Langkawi Sky Bridge
spots.label: Langkawi Sky Bridge

text.access_note: This is a ticketed attraction reached by cable car, so check the official site before you go for current access, tickets and weather closures.
text.description: Langkawi Sky Bridge is a curved walkway hanging from a single tall pylon on the top of Gunung Mat Cincang, 660 metres above sea level. It is 125 metres long and was designed with its bend so that the view changes as you walk along it. That is what makes it good for phone photos: every few steps the railings, the cables and the valley line up differently. The bridge opened to the public in 2005, closed in 2012 for upgrading, and reopened in 2015 (partially in February, with the SkyGlide finished in December 2015). It is a pedestrian bridge only, and it is fairly narrow, so you will often be sharing the deck with other visitors. There is a small triangular platform at each end where you can stop without blocking anyone. Use these for your longer pauses. The sloping pylon and its fan of cables make a strong shape against the sky, so try one shot that includes them. Keep another for the green hillsides and the drop below the railings. Hold the phone with both hands, keep strap and fingers clear of the lens, and take a few frames of each view because people keep moving through. Because you reach the bridge from the cable car's Top Station, check the official site before you go for current access, tickets and any weather closures.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops apply here. Take the Langkawi Cable Car up to the Top Station. From there the SkyGlide inclined lift takes you down to the bridge in about two minutes. Alternatively, you can follow a steep mountain track on foot, which takes roughly 10 to 20 minutes and is less secure underfoot. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.geographic_location: The bridge is on the summit of Gunung Mat Cincang, on Pulau Langkawi, the main island of the Langkawi archipelago in Kedah, Malaysia. It links two hilltops next to the top of the Langkawi Cable Car.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and use the railing as a leading line that curves away from you. Put the pylon and cables on one third of the frame and leave the valley on the other. Crouch slightly for a low shot of the deck, and keep the phone clear of the mesh at the sides so it does not catch the wire.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Take your first photos here, then walk to either end platform for a view back along the curve.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the railing or a person, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky does not wash out. Skip panorama mode, because the bridge and other visitors move and it will stitch badly. Wipe the lens first, as mist or fingerprints cause haze.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the day if you can, when the bridge is likely to be quieter and the summit clearer. Cloud or mist can come in later and hide the view, so check the weather before you go up.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the curve of the deck, the pylon and the cables in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for pictures of people on the bridge, and the telephoto (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) for faraway hills and sea.

spots.name: Pantai Cenang
spots.label: Pantai Cenang

text.access_note: This is an open public square and beach with no charge mentioned in the guides; check the official site before you go if you have any doubts.
text.description:
Pantai Cenang is one of Langkawi's best-known stretches of white sand, and the easiest place to start is the central beach entrance, a public square called Pantai Chenang Plaza. A rainbow-coloured Pantai Chenang sign stands here, and behind it you can see the beach and the Andaman Sea. That makes a ready-made foreground for a sunset picture: the sign tells people where they are, and the sea and sky fill the rest of the frame.

Guides name this square as the classic sunset backdrop, so expect company. One blog says people gather opposite Cenang Mall to watch the sun go down, and it is busiest at weekends. If you want a clear view of the sign, arrive well before the sun is low and take your pictures first, then relax and enjoy the colours.

Face west toward the sea. Stand a few steps back from the sign so it sits low in the frame, with the horizon about a third of the way up. If the crowd is thick, move along the sand and shoot at a slight angle rather than waiting for a gap. If you would rather be away from the busy sign area, Casa del Mar is described as a less crowded section of the beach, with the boardwalk and sea in view.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this part of Langkawi, so arrange your own transport from wherever you are staying on the island. Head for Pantai Chenang Plaza, the central beach entrance. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.geographic_location: Pantai Cenang is on Langkawi and looks out toward the Andaman Sea. The photo spot is the central beach entrance; one blog places it opposite Cenang Mall.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line, keeping it level. Place the sign low in the frame as a foreground. If the square is crowded, take a few steps along the sand and angle the shot slightly. A less crowded part of the beach near Casa del Mar has the boardwalk and sea in view, if you want to get away from the sign area.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Pantai Chenang Plaza (central beach entrance, facing west toward the sea). The rainbow-coloured Pantai Chenang sign in the foreground with the beach and the sunset over the Andaman Sea behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bright sky near the sun, then slide the exposure down a little so the colours stay rich and the sky does not wash out. The sign may then look darker, which suits a silhouette. For a properly lit sign, take a second shot earlier, tapping on the sign to focus. Take a Live Photo too if you want a little movement from the waves.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around sunset. One blog gives roughly 7.15–7.40pm as the usual window, but check the sunset time for your date and arrive early to claim a spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the sign with the beach and sunset behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more sky and sea, or to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the sun low over the water.

text.access_note: This is likely a ticketed attraction, so check the official site before you go for entry and photography rules.
text.description: Underwater World Langkawi is rank 4 on this map. It is an aquarium, so most of your photos will be of what lives behind the glass rather than of the building. The main challenge is the light. Tanks are usually dim, and the glass picks up reflections from your own clothes and from lights behind you. Move close to the glass, hold the top of your phone almost against it, and the reflections mostly disappear. Fish move quickly, so take several frames and keep the best one. Wide views of a big tank work well in ultra-wide. Single animals suit the default lens (1x) or a little zoom. Outside, a quick shot of the entrance makes a nice record of the visit. Please keep the flash off. It reflects in the glass and can bother the animals. Rules on photography, bags and tripods inside can differ, and entry is likely to be ticketed, so check the official site before you go. I have no further history, size or date details to share for this spot.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed for this spot, so use the map and follow the phone icon to the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the attraction itself, so there is no extra walk and no bearing to follow once you are there. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.geographic_location: Underwater World Langkawi is on the island of Langkawi, Malaysia. Use the map coordinates to find its exact position.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the horizon of the water or the tank edge on a grid line. Put your phone against or very near the glass to cut reflections. Leave some space in front of a moving animal so it has room to swim into the frame. For an outside shot, include the whole entrance and a little of the surroundings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Inside, stand close to the glass, square-on, rather than at an angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the animal to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the bright water washes out. If the tank is very dark, let night mode work and hold still. Try Live Photos or motion for fish, then choose the sharpest frame. Keep the flash off.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go when you have time to wait for a good moment. Fewer people around means you can reach the glass more easily, so a quieter time of day is usually easier. Outside, daylight gives the best entrance shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for large tanks and for the entrance, and the default lens (1x) for most animal shots. Try 2x or more if your phone has it, for a single fish, but expect softer pictures in dim light.
